opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the framing of intelligence that's dominated the field for a long time is this idea of a single agent, a kind of brain in a box, and we ask whether it can match or exceed what a human can do. That's an interesting question, but it's not really the question that matters most when you think about systems at scale.

If you look at where intelligence actually shows up in the world, a lot of it is collective. A market is an intelligent system in some sense. Think about a city like New York: food arrives every day for millions of people, from all over the world, and nobody is in charge of that. No central planner computes it. It emerges from a huge number of local decisions, from prices, contracts, incentives, and people with their own preferences and private information interacting. That's a remarkable feat of coordination, and it's arguably more impressive than anything any single human brain does.

Economics is the field that has thought hardest about that kind of thing: how decentralized agents with different goals, scarce resources, and asymmetric information can produce good outcomes, or fail to. Mechanism design, incentives, contracts, and the role of prices as signals all become really central once you build machine learning systems that interact with lots of people.

And we are building those systems now. A recommendation system isn't just a predictor. It's sitting in a two-sided market between producers and consumers. If you ignore the fact that the people on both sides are strategic, that they have their own incentives, that they'll adapt to what your algorithm does, you get pathologies. You get things that look good on a test set and then do something quite bad in the world.

So for me the engineering goal isn't just "make an artificial human." It's to build systems, networks of humans and computers together, that create value, are fair, and handle uncertainty and scarcity sensibly. When you put it that way, you need statistics, because there's uncertainty everywhere. You need computer science, because it has to scale. And you need economics, because there are many agents with their own interests and you have to think about incentives and equilibria. I'd say that's really the emerging discipline: the blend of those three. Machine learning on its own has been a bit too focused on the single-agent, pattern-recognition view, and economics gives you the vocabulary for the social, collective side of intelligence.

r001.rationale: It connects economics and machine learning to systems involving many people, describing networks of humans and computers and intelligence emerging from many interacting agents.

r002.rationale: It identifies producers and consumers as participants with their own incentives and argues that systems must account for their strategic behavior and adaptation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that when people talk about intelligence, they almost always have a single agent in mind. There's a brain, or a computer, and it perceives, it reasons, it acts. And that's been the framing in AI from the very beginning — build a thing that can do what a human can do. But if you step back and look at where intelligence actually shows up in the world at scale, it's not in individual heads. It's in collectives. It's in markets, in supply chains, in cities, in the way millions of people who've never met each other manage to get food onto the shelves every morning. Nobody designed that. No single mind understands it. And yet it works, most of the time, remarkably well.

So economics, for me, is the field that took that phenomenon seriously. It asked: how do you get coherent, adaptive, even intelligent-looking behavior out of a large number of agents who have limited information, who have their own preferences, who are often in conflict with each other, and who are all making decisions under uncertainty? That's exactly the problem we're going to face as these learning systems get deployed everywhere — not one system, but millions of them, interacting, making recommendations, allocating resources, competing for the same scarce things.

And the thing that's missing from machine learning, as it's usually taught, is any notion of scarcity or of other agents. We have a loss function, we have data, we optimize. But in the real world, the data comes from people who have reasons for producing it, the predictions change the behavior of the people being predicted, and the resources you're allocating are wanted by someone else. The moment you put a learning system into that environment, you're doing economics whether you admit it or not. You're creating incentives. You're moving prices, implicitly or explicitly. You're affecting who gets what.

I also think economics has a kind of humility built into it that engineering often lacks. Economists have known for a long time that you can't centrally plan your way to a good outcome — the information just isn't available in one place. Hayek's point about prices as a compression of distributed knowledge is, to me, one of the deepest ideas about intelligence that's ever been articulated, and it has nothing to do with neurons. So when I hear people talk about building one giant model that knows everything and makes all the decisions, I think, well, we've run that experiment in the twentieth century, in a different form, and it didn't go well.

What I'd like to see is a merger. Take the statistical and computational tools we've developed — learning from data, dealing with uncertainty, scaling computation — and put them together with the economic ideas about mechanism design, incentives, equilibrium, and welfare. Then you can start to ask the right questions: not "is this model accurate?" but "does this system, deployed among people, actually make their lives better, and is it stable, and is it fair in some reasonable sense?" That's the engineering discipline I think we're missing, and it's where I've been trying to put my energy.

r001.rationale: The response pairs machine learning’s statistical and computational tools with economic ideas and describes intelligence at scale as arising among millions of interacting people in collectives.

r002.rationale: It says people produce data and that others want allocated resources, but it does not clearly argue that intelligent systems should respect humans specifically in both producer and consumer roles.

astra-6.text:
When you build a system involving millions of people and millions of decisions, intelligence isn’t just a matter of making accurate predictions. Those decisions interact. People have different goals, they have information that others don’t have, and they respond to what the system does. Economics gives us a language for thinking about those interactions.

Take a recommendation system. You might frame it as predicting what somebody wants to watch or buy. But there are also producers on the other side, whose livelihoods depend on what gets recommended. Your recommendations change what they produce, which changes what people can choose tomorrow. So you’re designing an evolving market, whether you acknowledge that or not. Prediction is one component; it isn’t the whole problem.

What interests me is how you combine learning with mechanisms that allow people to coordinate. How do you get useful information to flow? How do you align incentives? How do you account for costs that one person’s decision imposes on someone else? A system can be very good at optimizing a narrowly defined objective and still produce terrible outcomes collectively.

So I don’t think intelligence at scale should be understood simply as a bigger version of an individual brain. A market, for example, can coordinate activity without any one participant knowing everything. That’s a different kind of intelligence, and understanding how to build systems with that capacity requires economics alongside statistics and computer science.

r001.rationale: The response frames scale in terms of millions of people and decisions, and explains that combining learning with economic mechanisms addresses interactions among people.

r002.rationale: It considers producers’ livelihoods and how recommendations shape what people can choose, arguing that system design must account for these effects and collective outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
When you move from a single system making predictions to large numbers of systems interacting, you face a different set of problems. Each system’s decision changes the environment for the others. There are scarce resources, competing objectives, and information that some participants have and others don’t. Economics gives us a language for reasoning about those interactions: incentives, markets, equilibria, and mechanism design.

Think about a recommendation system. It’s tempting to describe its job as predicting what somebody wants. But recommendations also allocate attention and opportunity. They affect what producers create, which producers can earn a living, and what choices people will have in the future. The prediction is embedded in a larger economic system.

So, for me, intelligence at scale has to include the ability to coordinate decisions among participants whose interests aren’t identical. We need learning algorithms, but we also need to design the rules under which those algorithms interact. Economics is essential because it asks how individual decisions produce collective outcomes—and how we might make those outcomes better.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coordinating interacting systems and their economic effects on people, but it does not say that combining economic social intelligence with machine learning expands “scale” to mean numbers of humans.

r002.rationale: It notes that recommendations affect producers’ livelihoods and people’s choices, but does not clearly argue that intelligent systems should respect humans’ roles as both producers and consumers.
